meta.title: Fight Age Verification
meta.description: Make your voice heard against mandatory age checks and ID requirements that restrict children’s and young people’s rights online.
meta.shareImageAlt: Fight Age Verification campaign preview with the message that the internet should not require ID.
meta.keywords: age verification, online ID checks, social media age limit, children’s rights online, digital freedom, freedom of expression, EU age verification, Sweden social media age limit

hero.title: The internet should not require ID.
hero.lead: Governments are moving toward mandatory age checks online. In practice, that can mean showing ID to read, create accounts, or take part online.

definition.title: What is it?
definition.lead: Age verification means a service checks how old you are. That can sound simple, but it often turns into an ID check.
items: It often starts with child safety.
It can require ID, app verification, face checks, or similar tools.
Once the system exists, it can spread to more sites and services.

spread.title: How this spreads
spread.lead: Age checks rarely stay limited to one problem. Once ID checks become normal, the line can keep moving.

items.label: First
items.text: Social media and apps used by children.

items.label: Then
items.text: Forums, communities, search, and user-generated content.

items.label: Next
items.text: News, debate, learning resources, and niche interests.

items.label: Eventually
items.text: ID becomes a normal key for using the internet.

spread.adult: This affects adults too. Age checks can make lawful content, private browsing, and anonymous participation depend on showing ID.

issue.title: It is happening now
issue.lead: This is not a distant idea. The EU is building tools, and countries around the world are already moving. What starts as child safety can become ID checks for more and more of the internet.

items.label: EU
items.text: The Commission is pushing an EU age verification app, and the European Parliament has proposed a harmonised minimum age of 16 for social media.

items.label: UK and Australia
items.text: Australia is implementing social media minimum age rules, while the UK is pushing age assurance through the Online Safety Act.

items.label: Sweden
items.text: The government is investigating an age limit for children’s use of social media. The Social Democrats have also proposed a strict 15-year limit with ID checks.

questions.title: Why ID checks miss the point
questions.lead: Children should be protected online. But the answer cannot be to make ID checks the key to reading, learning, creating, or joining communities.

items.question: What are they trying to do?
items.answer: Make it harder for children to access social media or content seen as unsuitable.

items.question: What is the problem?
items.answer: Age checks sound simple, but they often become identity checks. Private reading, account creation, and participation can start depending on ID.

items.question: Who is affected?
items.answer: Young people seeking support, learning, following culture, or building something. Also adults who do not want lawful content, private browsing, or political debate to require ID.

items.question: What should be done instead?
items.answer: Target the harm directly: grooming, exploitation, fraud, harassment, poor moderation, and addictive or manipulative design.

scenarios.title: Who is actually affected?
scenarios.lead: An ID requirement sounds technical. In practice, it affects who can read, create, ask, debate, build, and belong.

items.label: The person who is struggling
items.title: The person who needs anonymous help
items.body: Someone who is struggling may need to seek support without first identifying themselves to a platform.

items.label: The person who wants to learn
items.title: The person who wants to learn online
items.body: Programming, AI, music, and games are often learned through open resources. ID checks make normal curiosity harder.

items.label: The visionary
items.title: The person who wants to start something
items.body: Young people should be able to launch side projects, create music, sell digital services, and build communities.

items.label: The curious person
items.title: The person who wants to understand the world
items.body: Young people need access to news, culture, politics, and niche interests to become genuinely informed.

targets.subject: Protect children online, but not through general ID checks
targets.copyFailed: Could not copy. Select the text manually.
targets.shortBody:
Hello,

I am writing to ask you to oppose mandatory age verification and general ID checks for using the internet.

Children should be protected online. But the answer cannot be to make ID checks the key to reading, learning, seeking support, joining communities, or taking part in debate.

This affects children and adults. Young people need room to ask for help, learn, create, follow news, build projects, and participate in society. Adults should not have to show ID to read lawful content, search privately, or take part in political debate.

Please support alternatives that target actual harm: grooming, exploitation, fraud, harassment, unsafe defaults, addictive or manipulative design, and weak enforcement. Child safety matters, but it should not be used to remove privacy, anonymity, and free expression online.

Kind regards,
[name]
targets.body:
Hello,

I am writing to ask you to oppose mandatory age verification and general ID checks for using the internet.

Children should be protected online. But general ID checks are the wrong route. They risk making the internet less private, less free, and harder to use for both young people and adults.

For young people, anonymous access to information, support, and communities can matter. That includes someone being bullied, someone unsafe at home, or someone who needs to ask about something sensitive. It also includes young people learning programming, music, AI, game development, or trying to start a side project. Much of that happens through open resources and forums.

For adults, age verification can mean that lawful content, private information seeking, and political participation start requiring ID. It also creates risks: data breaches, surveillance, profiling, and systems that later get used for more than they were built for.

I ask you to support solutions that target actual harm:

- grooming, exploitation, fraud, and harassment,
- better reporting, moderation, and law enforcement,
- safer defaults and less addictive or manipulative design,
- privacy-by-design without centralised ID databases,
- children’s right to seek information, express themselves, learn, and participate online.

Child safety must be taken seriously. But it must not become an argument for making the internet depend on identity checks.

Please say no to broad age verification and support alternatives that protect both children and fundamental freedoms.

Kind regards,
[name]

about.title: Why this page exists
about.body: Fight Age Verification is a small campaign page about broad age checks and ID requirements online. It explains the concern, links to sources, and helps people contact decision-makers.

sections.title: What the site does
sections.body: It summarizes the issue, shows who may be affected, and provides an editable email draft you can send from your own mail app.

sections.title: What the site is not
sections.body: It is not legal advice, a news service, an official government page, or an age verification tool. The sources are provided so readers can check the claims themselves.

sections.title: Core position
sections.body: Children should be protected online. But protection should target real harm instead of making ordinary internet use depend on general identity checks.

sections.title: Built by
sections.body: The site is built independently by Joel Hägvall. It is not affiliated with the people, parties, governments, or institutions mentioned on the site.

sections.title: Open source
sections.body: The source code is public for review, improvements, and suggestions.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.body: The site is built to collect as little information as possible. You can read it and use the email draft without logging in or identifying yourself.

sections.title: No account or ID collection
sections.body: You do not need to create an account, log in, or identify yourself to use the site. The site does not attempt to verify age or identity.

sections.title: Local preferences
sections.body: Choices such as language, theme, and selected recipients may be saved in your browser on your device. They are used to keep the site convenient for you and are not submitted through a form.

sections.title: Email function
sections.body: When you click Open email, your own mail app is used. The recipients, subject, and text are passed through a mailto link so you can review and edit the message before sending.

sections.title: Vercel Analytics
sections.body: The site uses Vercel Analytics for basic, aggregate traffic statistics, such as page views. It is not used for accounts, forms, or identity collection.

contact.title: Contact
contact.body: Found a mistake, a stronger source, a better recipient, or clearer wording? Send a suggestion.

sections.title: What to send
sections.body: Useful suggestions include factual corrections, source links, more relevant recipients, or wording that makes the page easier to understand.

sections.title: Keep it practical
sections.body: Concrete suggestions with a source link are easiest to check. Please include enough context to understand what should change and why.

sections.title: Built by
sections.body: The site is built independently by Joel Hägvall. For direct contact with the person behind the project, use the links below.

sections.title: Source code
sections.body: The project is open source. You can read the code or suggest changes on GitHub.
